item.title: [The Lancet] [Editorial] COPD as a life-course disorder: possibilities and practicalities
item.description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is predicted to affect an estimated 600 million people worldwide by 2050, an increase of 23% compared with 2020. It is one of the four largest contributors to the non-communicable disease burden according to the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health. And these estimates do not account for the many people with undiagnosed COPD or those in earlier stages of the disorder. item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Offline: Humanitarian health—the shameful silence
item.description: Joanne Liu was International President of Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) from 2013 until 2019. In her compelling memoir, Ebola, Bombs, and Migrants: Humanitarian Crises in a Security-Obsessed World (2026, written with André Pratte and first published in French in 2024), she recounts her time working at MSF and draws lessons for global health today. The premise for her argument is that 9/11 ushered in a securitised approach to humanitarian action, which “denied our common humanity”. item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] Horology and the heart
item.description: At the turn of the 17th century, the Venetian physician Santorio Santorio (1561–1636) described an instrument that rendered the pulse measurable. A weight was hung from a cord against a graduated scale and set swinging, the cord lengthened or shortened until the swing matched the beat beneath the doctor's fingers; a reading could then be taken from the scale. Santorio named it the pulsilogium, one of the first instruments of precision in medicine. Until then the pulse had been read by touch. item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Indonesia's fires are a health emergency
item.description: Since July, 2026, fires have burned across Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua. By Sept 9, Indonesia's Ministry of Health estimated that smoke had affected 12·5 million people;1 by Nov 2, facilities in seven provinces had recorded 401 586 acute respiratory infections, of which 91 913 were in children aged 5 years or younger.2 The smoke has crossed borders: on Oct 14, Singapore recorded a 1-h PM2·5 concentration of 284 μg/m3, its highest in 2026, while haze caused school closures in several Malaysian states and suspended face-to-face schooling nationwide in Timor-Leste for 3 days.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] The PSMAddition trial in metastatic prostate cancer
item.description: We read with great interest the report of the phase 3 PSMAddition trial by Scott T Tagawa and colleagues,1 which evaluated [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 added to androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) plus an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) in prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-positive metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. The investigators should be congratulated for completing a large and methodologically rigorous radioligand trial. The improvement in radiographic progression-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0·72; 95% CI 0·58–0·90) is clinically relevant.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] The PSMAddition trial in metastatic prostate cancer – Authors’ reply
item.description: We appreciate the interest in the PSMAddition study.1 Paolo Zaurito and colleagues discuss the study's control arm, toxicity of the triplet, and financial implications. item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Impact of high versus low fraction of inspired oxygen for anaesthetic washout and extubation on postoperative pulmonary atelectasis formation and oxygenation: importance of cumulative perioperative oxygen exposure. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 591–600
item.description: We read with interest the study by Paschold and colleagues1 showing that using a fraction of inspired oxygen (Fio2) of 70% for anaesthetic washout before extubation reduces postoperative pulmonary atelectasis and maintains oxygenation after tracheal extubation. We commend the authors for studying Fio2 management during emergence from general anaesthesia, a phase that is often overlooked, and for offering anaesthetists practical guidance on perioperative oxygen strategies. However, given the design of the study, some of the findings should be interpreted with caution.

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] The Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults and decommissioning the difficult airway trolley
item.description: In recent years, the ‘difficult airway’ trolley has sometimes been referred to as the ‘advanced airway’ trolley. As part of this evolution and in response to the Difficult Airway Society (DAS) 2025 guidelines for managing unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults,1 we propose that in certain areas this trolley is no longer necessary.

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] From population targets to personalised titration: translating within-patient electroencephalographic responses into clinical practice
item.description: Population-derived target ranges of drug concentrations or EEG indices are commonly used in clinical practice for the titration of anaesthesia. By definition, this inevitably results in a relative overdose for most patients and an underdose for a few. For accurate individualised titration of anaesthesia, suitable within-subject targets need to be established. item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Prognostic value of early renal recovery after cardiac surgery–associated acute kidney injury: a retrospective cohort study
item.description: Cardiac surgery–associated acute kidney injury (CSA-AKI) is common and strongly associated with adverse outcomes. Whether the timing of renal recovery adds prognostic information beyond AKI severity remains uncertain. We examined the association between renal recovery status after CSA-AKI and long-term mortality.

item.description: We thank Gee1 for a careful and constructive reading of our meta-analysis.2 Gee1 highlights an important distinction that was also acknowledged in our review: controlling the BIS more closely is not the same as demonstrating that patients experience better outcomes. For this reason, we identified multicentre trials powered for clinical endpoints and long-term cognitive outcomes as a priority for future research.

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Global Surgery and Anaesthesia—A Short Guide to Meaningful Involvement
item.description: In recent years, contemporary armed conflicts have multiplied in number, intensity, and duration, resulting in ever-increasing human losses. Climate-change-associated natural disasters are becoming more frequent and devastating. Epidemics, whether global or localised, such as the recurring Ebola outbreaks, regularly highlight the fragility of health systems. In many parts of the world, treatable diseases continue to cause preventable deaths due to a lack of resources, qualified personnel, or organised healthcare.

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Practical Approach
item.description: Critical care medicine has always been written in chapters. Some of its most influential textbooks have focused on the great syndromes and technologies that transformed our ability to save lives, and each has contributed to the extraordinary progress of modern intensive care. Yet, despite their importance, these textbooks often leave one fundamental question unanswered: what happens after survival?

item.title: [British Journal of Anaesthesia] Postoperative hypotension in patients recovering from noncardiac surgery: from detection to clinically meaningful interpretation. Response to Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 1846-7
item.description: We thank Wu and colleagues1 for their thoughtful comments on our observational study on postoperative hypotension in patients recovering from noncardiac surgery.2 Hypotension is a clinical sign. We agree that not all hypotension is equal; as with intraoperative hypotension,3,4 different endotypes of postoperative hypotension could exist with varying clinical importance. Nocturnal dipping, a decrease in blood pressure at night, is a sign of good long-term cardiovascular health rather than a risk factor for organ injury.
